segments.title: Theodore Roosevelt's blockade lesson from the War of 1812
segments.summary: Roosevelt's history of the War of 1812 uses Britain's blockade to argue that the United States needed naval readiness and a fleet capable of defending its long coastline.
segments.body: Britain tightened its blockade after Napoleon's reverses freed resources for the war against the United States. Royal Navy frigates watched American ports, merchant ships largely remained trapped, and commerce stopped along much of the coast. Privateers and the few regular cruisers that slipped through could win prestige, but they could not keep trade moving or prevent attacks along the seaboard. Roosevelt contrasts this weakness with Jefferson's failed attempt at peaceful economic coercion. His conclusion is that an ocean-facing state cannot substitute isolated tactical successes for the sea power needed to repel sustained pressure. That lesson helped shape later American naval doctrine.

evidence.note: The reading describes the British blockade, the limits of American privateers and cruisers, and Roosevelt's argument for a great fighting navy.

segments.title: Admiral Bacon on strategy and the peacetime arms trade
segments.summary: Admiral Reginald Bacon treats strategy as planning toward a desired result, then explains how armament firms built influence, markets, and foreign relationships during peacetime.
segments.body: Bacon defines strategy as planning toward a desired result, then applies it to business and the armaments industry. He rejects the simple claim that manufacturers necessarily wanted war, citing wartime taxation, capital costs, and the severe postwar slump at Armstrong Whitworth, Vickers, and Coventry Ordnance Works. In peacetime, company agents spent years building contacts abroad, learning local politics, and protecting a firm's reputation before orders appeared. Their work was commercial, but it also established a persistent national presence in foreign markets. That quiet presence amounts to diplomacy and falls outside narrower definitions of strategy that dominate policy debates.

evidence.note: The passage defines strategy, discusses armament manufacturers' incentives, and describes agents building foreign relationships over many years.

segments.title: Air-power theory, changing methods, and three-dimensional war
segments.summary: A Norwegian air-power study separates general principles from methods that change between wars, then compares the physical limits on armies, navies, aircraft, and submarines.
segments.body: The excerpt warns against treating the methods of one war as permanent principles because each conflict presents a different mix of geography and technology. Armies must work around rivers, mountains, mud, and floods, while fleets contend with coasts, rocks, gales, fog, and heavy seas. Aircraft can move vertically but still face weather, icing, and limited fuel. These constraints make the physical medium part of doctrine rather than a minor technical detail. Submarines also maneuver in three dimensions, which weakens the claim that this feature belongs uniquely to air warfare.

evidence.note: The discussion distinguishes principles from methods, compares each service's movement constraints, and notes the submarine parallel to three-dimensional air warfare.

segments.title: Interwar Royal Navy preparation and threat assumptions
segments.summary: Joseph Moretz's study of interwar capital-ship planning shows why preparation had to precede unmistakable hostility and how plans depended on political and geographic assumptions.
segments.body: The first quotations from Moretz's study concern the timing and assumptions behind interwar naval preparation. Bertram Watson warns that waiting for Japan to display hostile intent would give it time to prevent Britain from completing its preparations. A. C. Bell expects Britain to control German overseas communications as it had in the First World War, but that expectation depends on Norway and France remaining secure. A familiar operational method could fail if bases, coastlines, or allied territory changed hands. The passage presents war planning as a chain of political, geographic, and logistical assumptions rather than a prediction about fleets alone.

evidence.note: The quotations argue for advance preparation against Japan and reveal that plans for controlling German communications assumed Norway and France would remain secure.

segments.title: Tactical means and the danger of assuming equal competence
segments.summary: A 1925 naval manual and a Trafalgar staff-appreciation example connect strategic plans to tactical means while testing assumptions about an opponent's skill.
segments.body: The 1925 Naval War Manual states that a strategic plan will fail unless it provides the means for tactical success. Admiral Chatfield's claim that a formal staff appreciation would have predicted defeat at Trafalgar exposes another planning problem: the method assumes an opponent of comparable skill. That assumption would overstate the French and Spanish fleets at Trafalgar, while Germany in the First World War required greater respect for technical seamanship. Technical skill does not guarantee sound naval strategy. The comparison ends with the Second World War judgment that the Italian fleet posed a more serious threat than Germany's surface fleet. Plans therefore have to test both material means and the competence of the people expected to use them.

evidence.note: The passage links strategic plans to tactical means, explains equal-skill assumptions in staff appreciation, and compares French, Spanish, German, and Italian naval competence.

segments.title: Strategy, operations, and tactics at sea
segments.summary: The closing framework separates policy-level strategy, theater campaigns, and battle tactics, then asks how well a land-derived operational level transfers to naval warfare.
segments.body: The quoted framework places strategy at the level where military force serves policy, goals are defined, forces are assigned, and limits are set. The operational level plans and conducts a campaign within a geographic theater in support of that strategy. Tactics governs the employment of forces in battle. This three-level hierarchy grew largely from land-warfare theory, so its middle category does not always map cleanly onto naval activity. The distinction still provides a useful way to ask whether a naval action shapes policy, conducts a campaign, or fights an engagement.

evidence.note: The excerpt defines strategic, operational, and tactical levels and Dr. Clarke questions how cleanly the land-derived operational level applies at sea.
